63	\section{Spatial Adaptive $K$ Threshold Sweep}
64	\label{sec:spatial_adaptive}
65	
66	Table~\ref{tab:adaptive_spatial} reports the adaptive $K$ threshold sweep on LIBERO-Spatial, complementing the Object sweep in Table~\ref{tab:adaptive}.
67	
68	\begin{table}[h]
69	\centering
70	\caption{Adaptive $K$ threshold sweep and Plan~A on LIBERO-Spatial ($n{=}3$ seeds unless noted). Same thresholds $\tau$ as Table~\ref{tab:adaptive}. Plan~A Pareto-dominates all variable-$K$ thresholds: highest SR at lowest avg\_$K$. $^\dagger$\,$n{=}2$ (seed 44 pending).}
71	\label{tab:adaptive_spatial}
72	\small
73	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
74	\toprule
75	$\tau$ & SR (\%) & avg\_$K$ & fast path (\%) & SR/SR$_{K{=}10}$ \\
76	\midrule
77	\textbf{Plan~A (ours)} & $\mathbf{35.0 \pm 1.0}$ & \textbf{2.0} & \textbf{2.4} & \textbf{102\%} \\
78	\midrule
79	P90$^\dagger$ & $31.5$ & 3.55 & 80.6 & 92\% \\
80	P75 & $32.7 \pm 1.5$ & 5.02 & 62.1 & 95\% \\
81	P50 & $32.0 \pm 1.7$ & 6.35 & 45.6 & 93\% \\
82	P25 & $31.7 \pm 1.5$ & 7.65 & 29.4 & 92\% \\
83	\midrule
84	Fixed $K{=}10$ & $34.4 \pm 1.5$ & 10.0 & 0 & 100\% \\
85	\bottomrule
86	\end{tabular}
87	\end{table}
88	
89	Plan~A ($K{=}2$ selective CRM) Pareto-dominates all variable-$K$ thresholds on Spatial: $35.0 \pm 1.0$\% at avg\_$K{=}2$ versus the best variable-$K$ threshold P75 at $32.7$\% with avg\_$K{=}5.02$. The variable-$K$ thresholds show a monotonic SR decrease from P90 to P25, contrasting with the non-monotonic Object pattern (P50 $>$ P25 $>$ P75). This confirms that the optimal correction frequency is task-difficulty-dependent and that the uncertainty signal is effective---but its optimal utilization is $K{=}2$ selective CRM rather than variable-$K$ expansion.
90

92	\section{Applicability Boundary: Stochastic VLA Diversity}
93	\label{sec:applicability}
94	
95	The multi-sample pipeline requires stochastic action diversity across samples. We test this prerequisite by comparing SmolVLA (flow-matching, 450M) with OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024openvla} (autoregressive tokenization, 7B).
96	
97	\begin{figure}[h]
98	\centering
99	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_diversity.pdf}
100	\caption{Per-DOF action variance (log scale) across $K{=}10$ samples for SmolVLA (flow-matching) and OpenVLA (tokenized). OpenVLA produces 8/10 identical samples at temperature $T{=}0.5$, with per-DOF variance below $10^{-30}$ for most dimensions.}
101	\label{fig:diversity}
102	\end{figure}
103	
104	Figure~\ref{fig:diversity} shows the contrast: SmolVLA produces meaningfully diverse samples across all action dimensions, while OpenVLA at temperature $T{=}0.5$ generates 8 out of 10 identical action sequences, with per-DOF variance below $10^{-30}$ for most dimensions.
105	This near-determinism arises from autoregressive token selection: the argmax decoding at each token position collapses the distribution to a single mode, and moderate temperature fails to overcome the peaked distribution.
106	
107	This result establishes an applicability boundary: multi-sample inference-time correction is specific to stochastic generative VLAs (flow-matching, diffusion). Tokenized VLAs lack the action diversity that selection and correction rely on.
108	The boundary is architectural, not a limitation of our method: any inference-time approach that draws multiple action candidates requires the base policy to produce diverse samples.
109

111	\section{Per-Task Analysis}
112	\label{sec:per_task}
113	
114	Table~\ref{tab:pertask} reports per-task success rates on LIBERO-Object (seed 42) for the VLA-only baseline, Argmin selection, and obs\_only at two magnitude bounds.
115	
116	\begin{table}[h]
117	\centering
118	\caption{Per-task success rate (\%) on LIBERO-Object (seed 42, 10 rollouts per task). Tasks ordered by obs\_only $\varepsilon{=}0.2$ improvement over VLA-only.}
119	\label{tab:pertask}
120	\small
121	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
122	\toprule
123	Task & VLA-only & Argmin & obs\_only 0.1 & obs\_only 0.2 \\
124	\midrule
125	chocolate\_pudding & 20 & 30 & 50 & \textbf{60} \\
126	ketchup            &  0 &  0 & 10 & \textbf{20} \\
127	bbq\_sauce         & 20 & 30 & \textbf{40} & \textbf{40} \\
128	salad\_dressing    & 20 & 10 & 20 & \textbf{30} \\
129	butter             &  0 & \textbf{10} & \textbf{10} & \textbf{10} \\
130	milk               & 10 & 10 & \textbf{20} & \textbf{20} \\
131	orange\_juice      & \textbf{30} & \textbf{30} & \textbf{30} & \textbf{30} \\
132	tomato\_sauce      & \textbf{10} &  0 &  0 & \textbf{10} \\
133	alphabet\_soup     &  0 &  0 &  0 &  0 \\
134	cream\_cheese      & \textbf{10} &  0 & \textbf{10} &  0 \\
135	\bottomrule
136	\end{tabular}
137	\end{table}
138	
139	Improvement concentrates on medium-difficulty tasks.
140	The largest improvements appear on tasks where the frozen VLA partially succeeds but makes correctable errors: chocolate\_pudding (+40\,pp, from 20\% to 60\%), bbq\_sauce and ketchup (+20\,pp each), and salad\_dressing (+10\,pp).
141	These four tasks account for 9 of the 10 additional successes.
142	Conversely, four tasks (alphabet\_soup, cream\_cheese, tomato\_sauce, butter) remain at 0--10\% across all methods.
143	For these tasks, the base policy fails so completely that local action-level correction cannot recover a viable trajectory.
144	
145	Correction benefits tasks where the frozen VLA partially succeeds but makes correctable errors, rather than tasks where the base policy fails catastrophically or already succeeds reliably.
146	This pattern is expected for a residual correction approach bounded by $\varepsilon$: the CRM can fix small deviations in grasp pose or approach angle, but cannot recover from fundamental planning failures.
147	The concentrated improvement profile also addresses the question of effect size: the aggregate +10\,pp is not a uniform +1\,pp across 10 tasks, but a substantial +20--40\,pp on specific tasks diluted by tasks outside the correctable regime.

CRM inference adds only 0.28\,ms, making the correction overhead negligible. Plan~A's $K{=}2$ pipeline is 1.82$\times$ faster than the $K{=}10$ analysis baseline while achieving equal or higher success rate, because the 80\% reduction in VLA forward passes far outweighs the CRM overhead ($-$1.66\% net latency vs.\ $K{=}10$).

\section{Spatial Adaptive $K$ Threshold Sweep}
\label{sec:spatial_adaptive}

Table~\ref{tab:adaptive_spatial} reports the adaptive $K$ threshold sweep on LIBERO-Spatial, complementing the Object sweep in Table~\ref{tab:adaptive}.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Adaptive $K$ threshold sweep and Plan~A on LIBERO-Spatial ($n{=}3$ seeds unless noted). Same thresholds $\tau$ as Table~\ref{tab:adaptive}. Plan~A Pareto-dominates all variable-$K$ thresholds: highest SR at lowest avg\_$K$. $^\dagger$\,$n{=}2$ (seed 44 pending).}
\label{tab:adaptive_spatial}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
$\tau$ & SR (\%) & avg\_$K$ & fast path (\%) & SR/SR$_{K{=}10}$ \\
\midrule
\textbf{Plan~A (ours)} & $\mathbf{35.0 \pm 1.0}$ & \textbf{2.0} & \textbf{2.4} & \textbf{102\%} \\
\midrule
P90$^\dagger$ & $31.5$ & 3.55 & 80.6 & 92\% \\
P75 & $32.7 \pm 1.5$ & 5.02 & 62.1 & 95\% \\
P50 & $32.0 \pm 1.7$ & 6.35 & 45.6 & 93\% \\
P25 & $31.7 \pm 1.5$ & 7.65 & 29.4 & 92\% \\
\midrule
Fixed $K{=}10$ & $34.4 \pm 1.5$ & 10.0 & 0 & 100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Plan~A ($K{=}2$ selective CRM) Pareto-dominates all variable-$K$ thresholds on Spatial: $35.0 \pm 1.0$\% at avg\_$K{=}2$ versus the best variable-$K$ threshold P75 at $32.7$\% with avg\_$K{=}5.02$. The variable-$K$ thresholds show a monotonic SR decrease from P90 to P25, contrasting with the non-monotonic Object pattern (P50 $>$ P25 $>$ P75). This confirms that the optimal correction frequency is task-difficulty-dependent and that the uncertainty signal is effective---but its optimal utilization is $K{=}2$ selective CRM rather than variable-$K$ expansion.


\section{Applicability Boundary: Stochastic VLA Diversity}
\label{sec:applicability}

The multi-sample pipeline requires stochastic action diversity across samples. We test this prerequisite by comparing SmolVLA (flow-matching, 450M) with OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024openvla} (autoregressive tokenization, 7B).

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_diversity.pdf}
\caption{Per-DOF action variance (log scale) across $K{=}10$ samples for SmolVLA (flow-matching) and OpenVLA (tokenized). OpenVLA produces 8/10 identical samples at temperature $T{=}0.5$, with per-DOF variance below $10^{-30}$ for most dimensions.}
\label{fig:diversity}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:diversity} shows the contrast: SmolVLA produces meaningfully diverse samples across all action dimensions, while OpenVLA at temperature $T{=}0.5$ generates 8 out of 10 identical action sequences, with per-DOF variance below $10^{-30}$ for most dimensions.
This near-determinism arises from autoregressive token selection: the argmax decoding at each token position collapses the distribution to a single mode, and moderate temperature fails to overcome the peaked distribution.

This result establishes an applicability boundary: multi-sample inference-time correction is specific to stochastic generative VLAs (flow-matching, diffusion). Tokenized VLAs lack the action diversity that selection and correction rely on.
The boundary is architectural, not a limitation of our method: any inference-time approach that draws multiple action candidates requires the base policy to produce diverse samples.

\label{sec:per_task}

\midrule

milk               & 10 & 10 & \textbf{20} & \textbf{20} \\
orange\_juice      & \textbf{30} & \textbf{30} & \textbf{30} & \textbf{30} \\
tomato\_sauce      & \textbf{10} &  0 &  0 & \textbf{10} \\
alphabet\_soup     &  0 &  0 &  0 &  0 \\
cream\_cheese      & \textbf{10} &  0 & \textbf{10} &  0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Improvement concentrates on medium-difficulty tasks.
The largest improvements appear on tasks where the frozen VLA partially succeeds but makes correctable errors: chocolate\_pudding (+40\,pp, from 20\% to 60\%), bbq\_sauce and ketchup (+20\,pp each), and salad\_dressing (+10\,pp).
These four tasks account for 9 of the 10 additional successes.
Conversely, four tasks (alphabet\_soup, cream\_cheese, tomato\_sauce, butter) remain at 0--10\% across all methods.
For these tasks, the base policy fails so completely that local action-level correction cannot recover a viable trajectory.

Correction benefits tasks where the frozen VLA partially succeeds but makes correctable errors, rather than tasks where the base policy fails catastrophically or already succeeds reliably.
This pattern is expected for a residual correction approach bounded by $\varepsilon$: the CRM can fix small deviations in grasp pose or approach angle, but cannot recover from fundamental planning failures.
The concentrated improvement profile also addresses the question of effect size: the aggregate +10\,pp is not a uniform +1\,pp across 10 tasks, but a substantial +20--40\,pp on specific tasks diluted by tasks outside the correctable regime.


\section{Latency Breakdown}
\label{sec:latency}

Table~\ref{tab:latency} reports per-component wall-clock timing under batched inference on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 (CUDA 12.8, $N{=}1{,}000$ runs).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Per-step latency breakdown (ms, batched inference). CRM inference adds 0.28\,ms ($<$\,0.1\% overhead). Plan~A fast path runs at ${\sim}$4.0\,Hz; full path at ${\sim}$2.2\,Hz.}
\label{tab:latency}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
Component & Mean (ms) \\
\midrule
VLA E2E $K{=}1$ (batched) & 256.5 \\
VLA E2E $K{=}10$ (batched) & 253.2 \\
CRM forward & 0.28 \\
\midrule
Plan~A fast path ($K{=}2$, no CRM) & 252.9 \\
Plan~A full path ($K{=}2$ + CRM) & 459.6 \\
\midrule
Adaptive speedup vs.\ $K{=}10$ & $1.82{\times}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Under batched inference with shared KV cache, $K{=}2$ latency (${\sim}$253\,ms) is comparable to $K{=}1$ (${\sim}$257\,ms) because the flow-matching denoising of both samples runs in parallel. CRM inference adds only 0.28\,ms, making the correction overhead negligible. Plan~A's $K{=}2$ pipeline is 1.82$\times$ faster than the $K{=}10$ analysis baseline while achieving equal or higher success rate, because the 80\% reduction in VLA forward passes far outweighs the CRM overhead ($-$1.66\% net latency vs.\ $K{=}10$).
